n: Josiah held a Passover in Jerusalem on the fourteenth day of the first month — the proper time, unlike Hezekiah’s delayed one.

f.w: the fourteenth day of the first month

n: He assigned the priests to their duties and encouraged them in their temple service.

He told the Levites, who taught Israel, to put the holy ark in Solomon’s temple — no more carrying it on their shoulders — and serve God and His people. This is the last mention of the ark in the Old Testament historical books.

f.w: Put the holy ark in the house
f.g: The ark may have been removed during Manasseh’s reign; it vanishes from history after this.

f.w: the Levites that taught all Israel

n: Prepare by your family divisions according to the written instructions of David and Solomon.
Stand in the holy place in groups to serve each family of the people.
Slaughter the Passover lambs, purify yourselves, and prepare for your fellow Israelites to obey the Lord’s word through Moses.
Josiah personally donated 30,000 lambs and goats and 3,000 cattle for the people’s Passover — from his own possessions.
His officials gave willingly too. The temple leaders Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel gave the priests 2,600 small animals and 300 cattle.
Levite leaders gave 5,000 small animals and 500 cattle for the Levites’ Passover offerings.
With everything ready, priests and Levites took their places according to the king’s command.
They slaughtered the Passover lambs; the priests sprinkled the blood and the Levites skinned the animals.
They set aside the burnt-offering portions to distribute by family groups, as Moses’ law prescribed, and did the same with the cattle.
They roasted the Passover lambs as the law required and boiled the other holy offerings in pots, quickly serving everyone.
Since the priests were busy with offerings until night, the Levites prepared the meal for themselves and the priests.
The singers and gatekeepers stayed at their posts because their fellow Levites prepared their portions. Everyone served in his place.
All the Lord’s service was completed that day, as King Josiah commanded.
Israel kept the Passover and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread.
No Passover like this had been kept since Samuel’s day — not even under any king. Its faithfulness to the law, its scale, and its inclusion of all Israel set it apart.

f.w: from the days of Samuel the prophet

n: This Passover took place in Josiah’s eighteenth year — the same year the book of the law was found.
Years later (609 BC), Pharaoh Necho marched north to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates, helping Assyria against Babylon. Josiah went out to stop him.

f.g: A key city on the upper Euphrates, where Babylon decisively defeated Egypt in 605 BC.

n: Necho sent a message: “I’m not here to fight you but another kingdom. God told me to hurry. Stop opposing God, who is with me, or He will destroy you.”

f.w: forbear thee from meddling with God
f.g: Stop interfering with what God is doing.

n: Josiah refused to turn back, disguised himself for battle (as Ahab once did), ignored God’s words through Necho, and fought in the valley of Megiddo. Even a righteous man can misjudge where God’s voice is coming from.

f.g: A famous battlefield; later associated with ‘Armageddon.’

n: Archers shot Josiah, and he told his servants, “Take me away — I’m badly wounded.”
They moved him to his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried in his ancestors’ tombs. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned him.
Jeremiah composed laments for Josiah, and singers commemorated him for generations. His death became a symbol of national mourning.

f.g: A collection of laments, not necessarily the biblical book of Lamentations.

n: Josiah’s other deeds and his loyal devotion, in keeping with God’s law…

f.g: His acts of covenant faithfulness (Hebrew ḥasadim).

n: …from beginning to end, are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
